As a follow up to this series of posts, here is a version of the SIR model
that you can experiment with directly on this page, without needing to know
any computer programming.  Move the sliders and the solution is recomputed in
your browser.

If you arrived here and haven't already read the series of posts on this
topic, I recommend that you [start at the beginning](/2020/03/17/SIR_model.html).

The model is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dS}{dt} & = -\beta I \frac{S}{N} \\
\frac{dI}{dt} & = \beta I \frac{S}{N}-\gamma I \\
\frac{dR}{dt} & = \gamma I
\end{aligned}
$$

with $N=1$, so $S$, $I$, and $R$ are fractions of the population.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof beta = Inputs.range([0.01, 1], {value: 0.25, step: 0.01, label: "β (contact rate)"})
viewof gamma = Inputs.range([0.01, 0.5], {value: 0.05, step: 0.005, label: "γ (recovery rate)"})
viewof I0 = Inputs.range([1e-6, 0.01], {value: 1e-4, step: 1e-6, label: "I(0)"})
viewof T = Inputs.range([10, 365], {value: 200, step: 1, label: "Days"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Classical 4th-order Runge-Kutta for the SIR system with N = 1.
sol = {
  const f = ([S, I, R]) => [-beta * I * S, beta * I * S - gamma * I, gamma * I];
  const dt = 0.1;
  const nsteps = Math.round(T / dt);
  let u = [1 - I0, I0, 0];
  const out = [{t: 0, S: u[0], I: u[1], R: u[2]}];
  const axpy = (a, x, y) => y.map((yi, i) => yi + a * x[i]);
  for (let n = 1; n <= nsteps; n++) {
    const k1 = f(u);
    const k2 = f(axpy(dt / 2, k1, u));
    const k3 = f(axpy(dt / 2, k2, u));
    const k4 = f(axpy(dt, k3, u));
    u = u.map((ui, i) => ui + dt / 6 * (k1[i] + 2 * k2[i] + 2 * k3[i] + k4[i]));
    out.push({t: n * dt, S: u[0], I: u[1], R: u[2]});
  }
  return out;
}

peak = sol.reduce((a, b) => (b.I > a.I ? b : a))

Plot.plot({
  width: 700,
  height: 400,
  x: {label: "Time (days)"},
  y: {label: "Fraction of population", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["S", "I", "R"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0]),
    ...["S", "I", "R"].map(k =>
      Plot.line(sol, {x: "t", y: k, stroke: () => k, strokeWidth: 2})),
    Plot.ruleX([peak.t], {strokeDasharray: "4,4", stroke: "gray"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Basic reproduction number R₀ = β/γ = **${(beta / gamma).toFixed(2)}**.
The infection peak (dashed line) is at day ${peak.t.toFixed(1)}, where
I = ${peak.I.toFixed(3)} and S = ${peak.S.toFixed(3)}
(theory predicts S = γ/β = ${(gamma / beta).toFixed(3)} at the peak,
provided R₀ > 1).`
```
